newsitem.title: INDIA: India rupee to ease late '97/98-Standard Chartered.
newsitem.headline: India rupee to ease late '97/98-Standard Chartered.

text.p: The Indian rupee will start to weaken in late 1997/98 (April-March) but the currency holds little risk of a shock depreciation, Standard Chartered Bank treasury economist Mitul Kotecha said on Tuesday.

Kotecha, interviewed by Reuters during a visit to India, said there was a lot of pressure on the rupee to strengthen due to heavy capital inflows, which would make it overvalued on fundamental criteria such as trade and inflation.
But he expected the currency to be relatively stable for the next six months.
Then greater import demand in an accelerating economy, rising inflation and concern over competitive devaluations by South Asian neighbors will all weigh on the rupee, he said.

Indian exporters recently called for at least a seven percent rupee depreciation against the U.S. dollar, saying the local currency was overvalued and would aggravate a slowdown in the country's exports.
Kotecha, who monitors the Indian economy from London, said he expected the rupee to slip to 36.3 to the dollar by the end of 1997 and 36.6 by the end of the 1997/98 fiscal year (April-March).
The rupee traded around 35.75 to the dollar on Monday, after holding close to 35.85 for much of the past six months.
"There will be declines over the coming years but I do not see any big shocks, the RBI (Reserve Bank of India) is better at managing the currency," Kotecha said.
The economist said he foresaw India moving to full convertibility of the rupee in three years.
The rate of depreciation in the run-up to convertibility was likely to accelerate from 1.5 percent this year to 2.0-4.0 percent annually over the following years, he said.
The rupee now is convertible only on the current account, but two months ago former finance minister P. Chidambaram told the RBI to sketch the route to capital account convertibility.
To do that, India should have lower inflation, a smaller fiscal deficit, lower interest rates and political stability.
Hot money could quit India fast if investors were frightened by instability, and that could rock a newly convertible rupee.
"A high proportion of speculative inflows will be prone to political uncertainty," Kotecha said.

Kotecha forecast inflation, measured by the wholesale price index, at 8.4 percent year-on-year by the end of the fiscal year, up from 6.64 percent in the week ended April 12, the latest data available.
The RBI's bank rate, the new reference rate for the market, was likely to be around 0.5 percentage point higher than the current 11.0 percent as some upward pressure on rates was expected, he said.
He expected economic growth to be little changed from 1996/97's 6.7-6.8 percent, but expected extra momentum to build in the second half of the fiscal year.
"The economy will pick up later in the year and in the next fiscal year," he said.
But he said India needed to unlock infrastructure investment through tax incentives and a reduction in bureaucracy if it was to make the leap from seven percent growth to higher ground.
Kotecha described his bank as very bullish about India, both in general terms and specifically in the banking sector.

He said India's half-year credit policy statement announced on April 15 by the RBI, created monetary conditions to match the pro-growth, pro-investment 1997/98 budget that will be debated by parliament this week.
